ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the gods
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The gods are not explained here. The colony learns of them the way its people do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The colony's own book of the gods is a tab of the region window: what its people saw, were told and believe.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Whatever gods this world has, nobody explains them, and neither does this Almanac. Your colonists will see things, hear the old stories from visitors and neighbors, argue about what they mean, and sometimes be wrong; what they saw, were told and believe is written in the colony's own book of the gods, a tab of the region window. One setting, under The gods on the What's on page, decides whether the gods are there at all. How real they are is the same in every game: felt but never certain, though now and then one shows itself plainly, and what happens decides which.
What the colony's own people do for their gods is plain, though. Any altar, ritual place, sculpture or shrine of the colony's can be given to a god the colony knows (its button, Dedicate to a god): someone walks over and says the words, and a card says what the colony's people will do there from then on. They leave a small gift there now and then from what the stores can spare (a packed-away sculpture too, never one on show), come to pray there in hard times, and keep the god's feast day there. The place's inspect line shows what was last left there, what became of it, and what someone here holds the god loves; what becomes of a gift is what anyone can see where it lay (gone by morning, something else found in its place, or still lying there), and whoever finds it says whose doing they take it for. A prayer gives a small good mood, a little more said at the god's own place, and carrying a gift a small one for a day. In the book, a god's chapter opens with what the colony takes it to be, the colony's own sign of it drawn beside its name, once someone has told what it is; the same sign is on a god's card when the colony is sure who it was.
Each of your colonists holds the gods their own way. Who they are draws them toward one or another (their nature, the work they love, what they are, their past, the people they came from), never their family; praying, carrying gifts, keeping vows and feast days and what they see with their own eyes make it stronger, and neglect, unanswered prayers and broken vows wear it down. They pray to the god they hold most, and the devoted keep a small rite of their own for it now and then, a few seconds and a sentence. Two who hold gods set against each other may bicker about it. Something they saw can win someone over to another god, or leave them afraid of one; the afraid keep away from its place. A colonist's Culture tab says, in words, how they hold each god the colony has heard of and since when; in the book, a god's chapter says who here holds to it and who dreads it, as its keeper writes it down.
Your people also keep saints. With Ideology, a faith's deities are its saints (or its damned, feared and never prayed to): the ideoligion screen calls them by the faith's own word for them (saints, ancestors, exemplars, the damned), and in play a line under them names the god each is held to belong to, once your colony knows that god; the faith itself is never changed. When one of your colonists dies a remarkable death (carrying the wounded out of a fight, holding the line to the last, years of tending the sick, years of devotion, a vow kept to the end), the council may be asked to name them a saint of the colony's own: the person, never their family. Their grave, any statue you raise to a saint (its button, Raise to a saint) and the relic set aside when they are named are places the devoted go to pray now and then, and each year, on the day they died, the devoted keep their day at the grave. A god's chapter in the book lists the saints held to be its own.
